EMNLP 2023 FindingsTranslation evaluation

Exploring Context-Aware Evaluation Metrics for Machine Translation

Xinyu Hu, Xunjian Yin, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗Code ↗

Translation quality depends on surrounding sentences. Cont-COMET selects relevant document context and learns to score translations under the same conditions as human annotators.

01 / The research question

A sentence can be fluent and still be the wrong translation

A document gives a sentence more than background information. Earlier mentions can determine which person a pronoun refers to; later sentences can reveal which sense of a word was intended. An evaluator that sees only the current source, translation, and reference must judge without evidence that a human reader already has. The paper starts from this mismatch between the information used to annotate quality and the information used to predict that annotation.

Yet expanding the input is not sufficient. A sentence-level metric has learned which tokens its quality score describes. Prepending a paragraph at inference changes that input distribution and can blur the distinction between a good surrounding passage and a bad target sentence. The central tension is therefore selective access plus training: provide enough document evidence to interpret the target, while keeping the judgment focused on that target.

Which context reaches the evaluator?

Cont-COMET scores every reference sentence in the document by cosine similarity to the current sentence, discounted by α for each sentence of distance, keeps the highest-scoring ones up to a budget, and restores document order (Section 2.2). 03 / Inside the method

Context changes the representation; the target still determines the score

Cont-COMET retains COMET’s source–hypothesis–reference structure. Each stream is encoded with surrounding sentences, but the final sentence representation is pooled only over tokens belonging to the current sentence. A subtle choice matters: the translation hypothesis is surrounded by reference context, rather than context generated by the translation system. Otherwise, errors in neighboring machine translations could contaminate the evidence used to judge the target.

Selection combines semantic relevance with locality. Reference sentences receive a cosine-similarity score multiplied by a distance-decay factor. The metric selects high-scoring sentences, restores their original document order, and respects the encoder’s 512-token limit. Preceding and following sentences are both eligible. Context-aware fine-tuning then uses WMT2020 ratings aligned with document information; WMT2021 and WMT2022 provide the held-out evaluation. The interactive example isolates selection, with illustrative similarities rather than encoder outputs.

  1. 01

    Select relevant context

    Rank surrounding reference sentences by semantic similarity and distance, keeping the most relevant context within the encoder’s input limit.

  2. 02

    Encode the target sentence

    Combine preceding and following context with the source, reference, and translation; pool representations over the target sentence.

  3. 03

    Train with context

    Fine-tune COMET using contextualized examples and human ratings, matching the information available during human annotation.

04 / Reading the evidence

System-level gains can hide worse sentence judgments

  • 0.943

    WMT22 system correlation

    With six selected context sentences, Pearson correlation rises from 0.910 for COMET-21 to 0.943 on WMT22.

  • Training matters

    More context alone is insufficient

    Adding context only at inference improves system correlation but harms segment correlation; context-aware training largely resolves this trade-off.

The most revealing comparison is not simply Cont-COMET against COMET. On WMT22, adding three preceding and three following sentences only at inference raises system-level Pearson correlation from 0.910 to 0.952, but lowers segment-level Kendall correlation from 0.349 to 0.292. The trained six-sentence Cont-COMET setting reaches 0.943 and 0.354 respectively. Context-only inference can therefore improve how entire systems are ranked while making individual sentence judgments less faithful to human ratings.

Selection itself is a smaller contribution: the WMT22 ablation changes system correlation from 0.942 without selection to 0.943 with it, and segment correlation from 0.353 to 0.354. The stronger lesson is to train under the conditions in which the metric will be used. These correlations also do not directly establish that the model detects a particular discourse error; the paper evaluates agreement with human quality judgments rather than reporting an error-type detection benchmark.

Read the abstract

Previous studies on machine translation evaluation mostly focused on the quality of individual sentences, while overlooking the important role of contextual information. Although WMT Metrics Shared Tasks have introduced context content into the human annotations of translation evaluation since 2019, the relevant metrics and methods still did not take advantage of the corresponding context. In this paper, we propose a context-aware machine translation evaluation metric called Cont-COMET, built upon the effective COMET framework. Our approach simultaneously considers the preceding and subsequent contexts of the sentence to be evaluated and trains our metric to be aligned with the setting during human annotation. We also introduce a content selection method to extract and utilize the most relevant information. The experiments and evaluation of Cont-COMET on the official test framework from WMT show improvements in both system-level and segment-level assessments.
